blocks.text: Stand in the gallery of a large empty hall and shout once. You hear your own voice come back a moment later. That delay is not magic — it is the time the sound took to travel to the far wall and back, and from it you can calculate the size of the hall without moving a step.

blocks.markdown:
Sound is produced by a **vibrating body** — a drum skin, a guitar string, the vocal cords, a loudspeaker cone. The vibration pushes the surrounding air into alternating **compressions** (regions of higher pressure) and **rarefactions** (lower pressure), which travel outwards as a **longitudinal** wave.

Because the wave needs particles to pass the disturbance along, **sound cannot travel through a vacuum**. This is demonstrated by the classic bell-jar experiment: as air is pumped out, the ringing of an electric bell inside fades to silence even though the hammer is still visibly striking.

blocks.caption: Sound travels fastest in solids and slowest in gases, because closely packed particles with strong forces pass the disturbance on more quickly.

blocks.title: Factors affecting the speed of sound in air
blocks.text: Speed INCREASES with temperature (about 0.6 m/s for each degree Celsius) and increases slightly with humidity. It does NOT depend on the pressure of the air, nor on the loudness or frequency of the sound. These four points are asked directly in WAEC.

blocks.markdown:
### Echoes

An **echo** is sound reflected from a distant surface. The sound covers the distance to the reflector **and back**, so the total path is $2d$:

$$2d = v t$$

where $t$ is the time between making the sound and hearing the echo. Forgetting the factor of 2 halves or doubles almost every echo answer.

blocks.title: Finding a distance from an echo
blocks.prompt: A man claps his hands and hears the echo from a wall 0.50 s later. Taking the speed of sound in air as 340 m/s, calculate his distance from the wall.

steps.text: The sound travels to the wall and back, so the total path length is twice the distance.
Substitute the speed and the time.
Divide by 2 to get the one-way distance.
State the answer with its unit.

rows: Pitch — how high or low a note sounds
Frequency: higher frequency gives higher pitch
Loudness — how strong the sound seems
Amplitude: larger amplitude gives louder sound
Quality or timbre — why a flute and a violin differ on the same note
Number and relative strength of the overtones present

blocks.markdown:
### The audible range

A healthy young human ear responds to frequencies from about $20\ \text{Hz}$ to $20\,000\ \text{Hz}$. Below $20\ \text{Hz}$ is **infrasound**; above $20\,000\ \text{Hz}$ is **ultrasound**, used in medical scanning, in cleaning delicate instruments and in echo-sounding to measure the depth of the sea.

### Resonance in pipes and strings

When a vibrating column of air or a stretched string is driven at just the right frequency, a standing wave builds up and the sound becomes loud. This is **resonance**.

- **Closed (stopped) pipe** of length $L$: there is a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so the fundamental has $L = \frac{\lambda}{4}$, giving $f_0 = \frac{v}{4L}$. Only odd harmonics are produced.
- **Open pipe** of length $L$: antinodes at both ends give $L = \frac{\lambda}{2}$, so $f_0 = \frac{v}{2L}$. All harmonics are produced.
- **Stretched string** of length $L$ fixed at both ends: nodes at both ends give $f_0 = \frac{v}{2L}$.

blocks.title: Fundamental frequency of a closed pipe
blocks.prompt: A pipe closed at one end has a length of 0.25 m. Taking the speed of sound in air as 340 m/s, calculate its fundamental frequency.

steps.text: For a closed pipe, the fundamental fits a quarter of a wavelength into the pipe.
State the fundamental frequency with its unit.

blocks.title: Loudness does not affect speed
blocks.text: A gunshot and a whisper travel at exactly the same speed through the same air. Loudness is amplitude, and amplitude has no effect on wave speed — speed is fixed by the medium. Likewise a high-pitched note does not outrun a low one.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: Read echo questions carefully to see whether the quoted time is for the round trip or the one-way journey. "Hears the echo after t seconds" is always the round trip, so use 2d = vt. If the question gives the time to reach a wall, do not double it.

points: Sound is a longitudinal wave of compressions and rarefactions produced by a vibrating body and it cannot travel through a vacuum.
Sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids and slowest in gases; in air its speed rises with temperature but not with pressure or loudness.
For an echo, 2d = vt, because the sound covers the distance to the reflector and back.
Pitch depends on frequency, loudness on amplitude and quality on the overtones present; the audible range is about 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz.
Fundamental frequencies: closed pipe f₀ = v ÷ 4L, open pipe f₀ = v ÷ 2L and stretched string f₀ = v ÷ 2L.
